Business Critical analysis is analysis whose consequences are large enough that it is named,
registered and assured differently from everything else. NHSBSA holds the test for it, and this
playbook carries that test rather than a second one.

**The definition.** Business Critical Analyses are those "where a material error could directly
influence major policy, funding, statutory, regulatory or customer-impacting decisions, or cause
substantial financial, legal or service consequences."[^src-bca-assurance-journey-s1]

## How the answer is reached

You reach it on the **assurance level decision sheet**, which scores the analysis against six
impact dimensions from 1 to 4 and takes the highest. Analysis is Business Critical where **any one
dimension scores 4**. It does not need two, and a 4 anywhere carries the analysis to assurance
Level 4 whatever the likelihood of an error.

The six, in NHSBSA's own words:

| | Scores 4 where |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | The decision it informs impacts on major policy, funding, statutory or regulatory decisions |
| **Financial** | The amount of funding at risk exceeds £35 million, or the analysis directly informs major funding or investment decisions and the full financial consequences are not yet known |
| **Customers** | The impact on customers could affect individuals' rights, entitlements, eligibility, access to services, treatment, benefits or statutory obligations |
| **Legal or regulatory** | An error could create significant legal, regulatory or compliance exposure: legal challenge, judicial review, discrimination claim, statutory non-compliance, regulatory enforcement, significant financial penalties, reputational damage, or serious personal data breaches |
| **Public visibility and reach** | The analysis is the key evidence base for major policy, funding, regulatory or statutory decisions likely to be subject to intense public, ministerial, parliamentary, regulatory or media scrutiny |
| **Reputation** | Public trust would be at risk, because an error could cause a substantial and lasting loss of confidence arising from materially incorrect policy, funding, regulatory or statutory decisions |

[NHSBSA Business Critical Analysis: Navigating the Assurance Journey, 17 September 2026, section 5.
The same six are the impact dimensions on the decision sheet in Criteria for determining the level
of analytical risk v3, 10 September 2026. The financial threshold is marked "tbc" pending alignment
with the Standing Financial Instructions; the DHSC definition covers analysis where £40 million or
more is at risk.]

::: {.callout-important title="What does not, by itself, make analysis Business Critical" appearance="minimal"}
<br>
"Publication status, Board consideration, Official Statistics designation, media interest, national
visibility, FOI disclosure, ministerial interest or parliamentary scrutiny do not by themselves
justify a Level 4 score."[^src-bca-assurance-journey-s5]

Official statistics are assured under the Code of Practice whether or not they are Business
Critical. The two are different questions and a publication answers both separately.
:::

## When, and who

**When the Scope is complete**, before the Specification is written. That is the point the guidance
names, and the Scope is the first document that states what the analysis is for and what depends on
it, which is what the six dimensions ask about. Everything that follows from a yes, the register
entry, the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer and the enhanced assurance, takes time to arrange.

The guidance says the sheet **"can be used when the scope is completed"**.[^src-bca-assurance-journey-s5] **This playbook requires it**, because a designation reached after the
Specification is written cannot change the Specification, and because two analysts doing comparable
work should not be able to reach different levels with nothing recording why.

**Save the completed sheet and attach it to the Specification.** A recorded "no" is as useful as a
yes. An unrecorded one cannot be told apart from never having asked.

**The commissioner and the lead analyst score it together.** The commissioner knows what the
analysis will be used for and what depends on it; the analyst knows what it can bear. Where the two
disagree, escalate to the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead.

**The designation is a consequence of the impact assessment, not a separate judgement alongside it.**
You reach it by scoring the six dimensions on the decision sheet, which is the instrument you open
anyway to set your assurance level. It is a governance decision in the sense that it triggers
governance, not in the sense that somebody decides it somewhere else.

[^src-bca-assurance-journey-s5]: NHSBSA Business Critical Analysis: Navigating the Assurance Journey, 17 September 2026, section 5
